Laredo, Texas — Weeks after firefighters took their case to the Laredo City Council, the city's next labor contract with its firefighters remains unresolved, and the newest entries on the city's public meeting record show no deal has been announced.

As of mid-October, no new contract has surfaced on city agendas or in news coverage — meaning the city and the Regal Firefighters Association are still haggling over a proposed five-year deal covering pay and staffing, according to session titles on citizenportal.ai's Laredo feed. The latest public snapshot of the talks comes from Aug. 31, 2026 sessions.

At that council session, union president David Gonzales said the association had made concessions and substantially narrowed its demands in recent negotiations, but still needs additional funding — about 20 percent of the union's proposal — to guarantee four firefighters on every engine, every day, according to AI-generated meeting summaries from citizenportal.ai.

"We're asking for basically every fire truck to be mandated to be manned with 4 firefighters, every day," Gonzales told the council, arguing that four-person crews reduce workload, speed operations at major fires and medical calls, and protect both firefighters and residents.

Gonzales also pointed to a city-funded comparative pay study that cost "close to a $250,000," saying it showed Laredo firefighter pay and benefits trail other large departments in Texas. When council members asked whether the staffing goal required new hires or overtime, Gonzales said the union wants a sustained four-person staffing model — achievable through hiring, with planned overtime filling the gap until new firefighters are trained. The council moved to continue negotiations and directed staff and legal counsel to pursue the talks, the summaries say.

472 firefighters and a 24/72 future

Earlier, at a May 12, 2026 collective bargaining session, the union proposed a hard staffing floor of 472 full-time firefighters — a number the union says reflects the department's coverage area and gaps created when positions moved into administrative divisions, according to AI-generated summaries of that session from citizenportal.ai.

The union also laid out a long-term vision: moving the department to a 24-on/72-off shift schedule. Negotiators acknowledged it would take tens or hundreds of additional hires, continuous academy classes, and a multi-year fiscal plan — and that an upcoming retirement wave will require replacement hires in any case.

City negotiators acknowledged the safety concerns but called the target costly, noting academy throughput limits. They asked the union for phased hiring scenarios so the city can model budget and pension impacts. The union countered with a six-month window to backfill any vacancy once the staffing threshold is breached — and a novel penalty: if the city misses the deadline, it would keep paying retirement contributions for each unfilled position until the job is filled. City negotiators took the idea under advisement, the summaries say.

What's at stake for residents

This is not just a labor dispute — it is a public-safety equation.

Staffing is the heart of the union's pitch: four-person engine crews are the national standard. NFPA 1710, the standard for career fire departments, calls for a minimum of four firefighters per engine company. Under federal rules for interior firefighting (the "two-in/two-out" rule), an engine crew arriving with fewer than four members may have to wait for backup before entering a burning building — delaying rescue and suppression while a fire grows.

On the cost side, the city's proposed FY2026 budget put the fire department at about $84.2 million, up from $80.4 million — and city budget staff have said a 4 percent cost-of-living adjustment and negotiated increases for police and fire are built into the plan. Fire department staffing historically consumes more than 90 percent of its operating budget, so every hiring commitment is a long-term budget commitment for taxpayers.

The union's argument, in short: pay more now for people, or pay later in overtime, injuries, and slower response. The city's argument: the fiscal and training capacity isn't there to staff up overnight.

Questions still unanswered

  • Where exactly do the numbers stand now — and has either side moved since Aug. 31?
  • What would the additional staffing cost taxpayers per year, and how does that compare to the overtime bill the department is paying today?
  • Is the union's 472-firefighter floor still on the table, and how would academy classes scale to meet it?
  • Does the prior contract remain in force during negotiations, and would any new pay deal be retroactive?

Webb Watch 956 reviewed citizenportal.ai's Laredo feed this week and found no public record of a newer bargaining session on the firefighter contract after the Aug. 31 meetings — the most recent entries concern other city business, including Oct. 15 public-health briefings. With no deal announced, the watch continues.
